items.stem:
Read the passage below and answer the questions that follow.

Walking to School

1. Not long ago, most Indian children walked or cycled to school. Today, in many cities, a large number are driven in cars, vans or on two-wheelers, even when the school is only a kilometre away. Parents worry about traffic, safety and time, and so the short walk that was once a daily habit is disappearing.

2. Doctors say that this change has a cost. Children who walk or cycle get regular exercise without even noticing it. They arrive at school more alert, and studies suggest they concentrate better in the first lessons of the day. Children who are always driven miss this easy chance to stay fit, and many spend the rest of the day sitting.

3. There are other benefits too. Walking children learn to read their neighbourhood – to cross roads carefully, to recognise shops and landmarks, to greet neighbours. They become more confident and independent. Fewer cars at the school gate also mean less pollution and less of the dangerous crowding that every school knows at 8 a.m.

4. Some schools have found a clever solution called the "walking bus". A group of children walks together along a fixed route, picking up others at "stops" on the way, with two adults – one at the front and one at the back. Parents feel the children are safe, and the children enjoy the company.

5. Of course, walking is not possible everywhere. Some roads have no footpaths, and some children live far away. But where it is possible, the writer argues, the humble walk to school deserves to make a comeback.

(i) How did most Indian children travel to school in the past?
(ii) Why do many parents now drive their children to school?  (a) They worry about traffic, safety and time  (b) Children dislike fresh air  (c) Fuel is free  (d) Schools forbid walking
(iii) According to doctors, children who walk to school …  (a) need more medicine  (b) concentrate better in the first lessons  (c) get lower marks  (d) fall asleep in class
(iv) What "cost" does the writer mention in paragraph 2?
(v) Name two ways in which walking makes children more independent.
(vi) How does walking help the environment around schools?  (a) It has no effect  (b) Fewer cars means less pollution and crowding at the gate  (c) It increases noise  (d) More cars are needed
(vii) Which word in paragraph 3 means "places or buildings that are easy to recognise"?  (a) neighbours  (b) landmarks  (c) pollution  (d) crowding
(viii) What is a "walking bus"?
(ix) How many adults go with a walking bus?  (a) Four  (b) One  (c) Two  (d) None
(x) Why is walking not possible everywhere?
items.answer: (i) They walked or cycled. (ii) (a) They worry about traffic, safety and time (iii) (b) concentrate better in the first lessons (iv) Children who are always driven miss easy daily exercise and remain inactive. (v) They learn to cross roads, recognise landmarks, greet neighbours and grow confident (any two). (vi) (b) Fewer cars means less pollution and crowding at the gate (vii) (b) landmarks (viii) A group of children walking together along a fixed route with adults at the front and back, picking up others at stops. (ix) (c) Two (x) Some roads have no footpaths and some children live far away.
items.markingKey: (i) They walked or cycled. (ii) (a) They worry about traffic, safety and time (iii) (b) concentrate better in the first lessons (iv) Children who are always driven miss easy daily exercise and remain inactive. (v) They learn to cross roads, recognise landmarks, greet neighbours and grow confident (any two). (vi) (b) Fewer cars means less pollution and crowding at the gate (vii) (b) landmarks (viii) A group of children walking together along a fixed route with adults at the front and back, picking up others at stops. (ix) (c) Two (x) Some roads have no footpaths and some children live far away. (1 mark each, 10 marks.)

Read the survey report and answer the questions that follow.

A survey on buying handmade products was carried out in Jaipur in 2025. 1000 shoppers at a city fair were asked how often they buy handmade craft products. The results were: every month – 7%; a few times a year – 4%; only during festivals – 8%; never – 81%. The word "artisans" came up often in the discussion that followed the survey.

(i) Which response was the most common?  (a) only during festivals  (b) a few times a year  (c) never  (d) every month
(ii) Which response was the least common?  (a) every month  (b) only during festivals  (c) never  (d) a few times a year
(iii) How many shoppers at a city fair chose "every month"?  (a) 810  (b) 7  (c) 70  (d) 700
(iv) What percentage of shoppers at a city fair chose one of the two most common responses taken together?  (a) 81%  (b) 99%  (c) 89%  (d) 11%
(v) Did more than half of the shoppers at a city fair choose "never"? Give the figure.
(vi) Which of these statements is supported by the survey?  (a) "a few times a year" was chosen by more shoppers at a city fair than "never".  (b) Every response was chosen by the same number of shoppers at a city fair.  (c) "never" was chosen by more shoppers at a city fair than "only during festivals".  (d) The survey was carried out in Agra.
(vii) In the passage, the word "artisans" means …  (a) skilled workers who make things by hand  (b) separate into groups  (c) protect from waste or loss  (d) the pleasure of being with others
(viii) Suggest one reason why "a few times a year" may have been chosen by so few shoppers at a city fair.
(ix) What fraction of the shoppers at a city fair did NOT choose "every month"? Answer as a percentage.  (a) 19%  (b) 43%  (c) 7%  (d) 93%
(x) Rank the top three responses, starting with the most common.
items.answer: (i) (c) never (ii) (d) a few times a year (iii) (c) 70 (iv) (c) 89% (v) Yes – 81%, which is more than half. (vi) (c) "never" was chosen by more shoppers at a city fair than "only during festivals". (vii) (a) skilled workers who make things by hand (viii) Any sensible reason linked to the context (cost, habit, lack of access, awareness, time) – 1 mark. (ix) (d) 93% (x) never, only during festivals, every month

"Every Wednesday the postman brought the thick weekly magazine, and every Wednesday evening Ajji settled on her mat with her betel box beside her. items.stem:
Read the passage below and answer the questions that follow.

The Monsoon Kitchen Garden

1. When the first monsoon showers soak the dry earth, Meera's grandmother goes out to the small patch of ground behind their house. She does not buy seedlings from a nursery. Instead, she opens tins of seeds saved from last year's best plants – bottle gourd, okra, coriander, beans – and presses them gently into the wet soil.

2. Her kitchen garden is only a few metres long, but by August it is a tangle of green. Creepers climb the bamboo frame she builds every year, and small yellow flowers turn into pods and gourds. She uses no chemical fertilisers. Kitchen peels, dried leaves and cow dung are buried in a pit and turned into dark, crumbly compost.

3. Meera used to think the garden was old-fashioned. Then her biology teacher explained that saving seeds keeps alive local varieties that are suited to the region's soil and rain. Many such varieties have disappeared from farms, replaced by a few kinds sold in shops. In a small way, her grandmother's tins were a seed bank.

4. The garden also saves money and reduces waste. On many days, the family's vegetables come from just outside the back door, fresh and free of pesticides. Nothing from the kitchen is thrown out; it returns to the soil. Neighbours often leave with a bag of beans and come back with a bowl of something cooked from them.

5. This year, Meera has started her own corner of the garden. Her first okra plant is crooked and small, but she is proud of it. Her grandmother only smiles and says, "The soil teaches patience. Listen to it."

(i) When does the grandmother begin planting?  (a) When the first monsoon showers soak the earth  (b) In midwinter  (c) In peak summer  (d) During exams
(ii) Where does the grandmother get her seeds?
(iii) What is the bamboo frame used for?  (a) To dry clothes  (b) To keep goats out  (c) To hold compost  (d) For the creepers to climb
(iv) How does the grandmother make compost?
(v) Which word in paragraph 2 means "easily broken into small pieces"?  (a) chemical  (b) crumbly  (c) tangle  (d) creepers
(vi) Why did the biology teacher praise seed saving?
(vii) Why does the writer call the tins "a seed bank"?  (a) They store and protect local seed varieties for the future  (b) They are made of metal  (c) They are kept in a bank  (d) They contain money
(viii) Give two benefits of the kitchen garden mentioned in paragraph 4.
(ix) What do neighbours bring back after receiving beans?  (a) Fertiliser  (b) A bowl of something cooked from them  (c) Money  (d) A packet of seeds
(x) What does the grandmother mean by "The soil teaches patience"?
items.answer: (i) (a) When the first monsoon showers soak the earth (ii) From tins of seeds saved from last year's best plants. (iii) (d) For the creepers to climb (iv) She buries kitchen peels, dried leaves and cow dung in a pit until they turn into compost. (v) (b) crumbly (vi) It keeps alive local varieties suited to the region's soil and rain. (vii) (a) They store and protect local seed varieties for the future (viii) It saves money, gives fresh pesticide-free vegetables and reduces waste (any two). (ix) (b) A bowl of something cooked from them (x) Growing plants takes time; gardening teaches us to wait and care.
items.markingKey: (i) (a) When the first monsoon showers soak the earth (ii) From tins of seeds saved from last year's best plants. (iii) (d) For the creepers to climb (iv) She buries kitchen peels, dried leaves and cow dung in a pit until they turn into compost. (v) (b) crumbly (vi) It keeps alive local varieties suited to the region's soil and rain. (vii) (a) They store and protect local seed varieties for the future (viii) It saves money, gives fresh pesticide-free vegetables and reduces waste (any two). (ix) (b) A bowl of something cooked from them (x) Growing plants takes time; gardening teaches us to wait and care. (1 mark each, 10 marks.)

Read the passage below, based on the poem 'Nine Gold Medals', and answer.

"The whistle blew; the runners flew, / The crowd was on its feet; / But one went down, and with a frown / The others turned to meet / The boy who lay upon the track – / They did not race, they all came back."

Answer the following:
(i) What happened when the whistle blew?
(ii) What did "the others" do?  (a) They ran faster  (b) They cheered alone  (c) They left the track  (d) They turned back to help the boy who fell
(iii) Find an example of internal rhyme in the first line.  (a) "down" and "frown"  (b) "track" and "back"  (c) "blew" and "flew"  (d) "feet" and "meet"
(iv) Which quality do the runners show?  (a) Pride  (b) Compassion/kindness  (c) Selfishness  (d) Fear

items.stem:
Read the passage below and answer the questions that follow.

Walking to School

1. Not long ago, most Indian children walked or cycled to school. Today, in many cities, a large number are driven in cars, vans or on two-wheelers, even when the school is only a kilometre away. Parents worry about traffic, safety and time, and so the short walk that was once a daily habit is disappearing.

2. Doctors say that this change has a cost. Children who walk or cycle get regular exercise without even noticing it. They arrive at school more alert, and studies suggest they concentrate better in the first lessons of the day. Children who are always driven miss this easy chance to stay fit, and many spend the rest of the day sitting.

3. There are other benefits too. Walking children learn to read their neighbourhood – to cross roads carefully, to recognise shops and landmarks, to greet neighbours. They become more confident and independent. Fewer cars at the school gate also mean less pollution and less of the dangerous crowding that every school knows at 8 a.m.

4. Some schools have found a clever solution called the "walking bus". A group of children walks together along a fixed route, picking up others at "stops" on the way, with two adults – one at the front and one at the back. Parents feel the children are safe, and the children enjoy the company.

5. Of course, walking is not possible everywhere. Some roads have no footpaths, and some children live far away. But where it is possible, the writer argues, the humble walk to school deserves to make a comeback.

(i) Why do many parents now drive their children to school?  (a) Schools forbid walking  (b) They worry about traffic, safety and time  (c) Fuel is free  (d) Children dislike fresh air
(ii) According to doctors, children who walk to school …  (a) fall asleep in class  (b) concentrate better in the first lessons  (c) need more medicine  (d) get lower marks
(iii) What "cost" does the writer mention in paragraph 2?
(iv) Name two ways in which walking makes children more independent.
(v) Which word in paragraph 3 means "places or buildings that are easy to recognise"?  (a) neighbours  (b) crowding  (c) landmarks  (d) pollution
(vi) What is a "walking bus"?
(vii) How many adults go with a walking bus?  (a) Two  (b) Four  (c) One  (d) None
(viii) Why is walking not possible everywhere?
(ix) The writer's purpose in the passage is mainly to …  (a) persuade readers that walking to school should return where possible  (b) describe a holiday  (c) sell cars  (d) warn against exercise
(x) What does the phrase "the humble walk" suggest?
items.answer: (i) (b) They worry about traffic, safety and time (ii) (b) concentrate better in the first lessons (iii) Children who are always driven miss easy daily exercise and remain inactive. (iv) They learn to cross roads, recognise landmarks, greet neighbours and grow confident (any two). (v) (c) landmarks (vi) A group of children walking together along a fixed route with adults at the front and back, picking up others at stops. (vii) (a) Two (viii) Some roads have no footpaths and some children live far away. (ix) (a) persuade readers that walking to school should return where possible (x) Walking is simple and ordinary but valuable.
items.markingKey: (i) (b) They worry about traffic, safety and time (ii) (b) concentrate better in the first lessons (iii) Children who are always driven miss easy daily exercise and remain inactive. (iv) They learn to cross roads, recognise landmarks, greet neighbours and grow confident (any two). (v) (c) landmarks (vi) A group of children walking together along a fixed route with adults at the front and back, picking up others at stops. (vii) (a) Two (viii) Some roads have no footpaths and some children live far away. (ix) (a) persuade readers that walking to school should return where possible (x) Walking is simple and ordinary but valuable. (1 mark each, 10 marks.)

items.stem:
Read the survey report and answer the questions that follow.

A survey on care for elderly neighbours was carried out in Dehradun in 2025. 200 residents of a housing society were asked how often they spend time with elderly people in their area. The results were: daily – 31%; every week – 15%; once a month – 14%; hardly ever – 40%. The word "companionship" came up often in the discussion that followed the survey.

(i) Which response was the most common?  (a) daily  (b) hardly ever  (c) once a month  (d) every week
(ii) Which response was the least common?  (a) hardly ever  (b) every week  (c) once a month  (d) daily
(iii) How many residents of a housing society chose "hardly ever"?  (a) 28  (b) 80  (c) 40  (d) 800
(iv) By how many percentage points does "hardly ever" differ from "once a month"?  (a) 54  (b) 23  (c) 26  (d) 31
(v) What percentage of residents of a housing society chose one of the two most common responses taken together?  (a) 71%  (b) 81%  (c) 29%  (d) 40%
(vi) Did more than half of the residents of a housing society choose "hardly ever"? Give the figure.
(vii) In the passage, the word "companionship" means …  (a) the pleasure of being with others  (b) calming  (c) protect from waste or loss  (d) more than is necessary or healthy
(viii) Suggest one reason why "once a month" may have been chosen by so few residents of a housing society.
(ix) Write one suggestion the organisers could make, based on the survey on care for elderly neighbours.
(x) Rank the top three responses, starting with the most common.
items.answer: (i) (b) hardly ever (ii) (c) once a month (iii) (b) 80 (iv) (c) 26 (v) (a) 71% (vi) No – 40%, which is less than half. (vii) (a) the pleasure of being with others (viii) Any sensible reason linked to the context (cost, habit, lack of access, awareness, time) – 1 mark. (ix) Any practical suggestion that follows from the figures – 1 mark. (x) hardly ever, daily, every week
items.markingKey: (i) (b) hardly ever (ii) (c) once a month (iii) (b) 80 (iv) (c) 26 (v) (a) 71% (vi) No – 40%, which is less than half. (vii) (a) the pleasure of being with others (viii) Any sensible reason linked to the context (cost, habit, lack of access, awareness, time) – 1 mark. (ix) Any practical suggestion that follows from the figures – 1 mark. (x) hardly ever, daily, every week (1 mark each.)
